name: Commodity skewness factor

origin.source_title: The skewness of commodity futures returns (Journal of Banking and Finance 86, 143-158)

how_it_works.simple: Buy the commodities whose past year had more sudden drops than jumps, and sell those with more sudden jumps, because people overpay for lottery-like jumps.
how_it_works.analogy: Like selling lottery tickets: buyers pay extra for the small chance of a big win.
how_it_works.precise: Each month, compute the skewness of the past 12 months of daily returns per commodity; long the fifth with the most negative skew, short the fifth with the most positive. 27 commodities, 1987 to 2014: 8.01% a year, Sharpe 0.78, alpha 6.21% after standard commodity factors.

rule: Monthly: skewness of 252 daily returns; long the lowest-skew fifth, short the highest-skew fifth, equal weights.
data_needed: Daily futures returns for 20 or more commodities
economic_rationale: Investors with a taste for positive skew (cumulative prospect theory) overpay for right-skewed commodities; selective hedging adds to it.
why_it_might_fail: Needs a broad cross-section we do not have for free; skewness estimates are noisy.

reported_results.source: Fernandez-Perez, Frijns, Fuertes and Miffre (2018), accepted manuscript, Table IV
reported_results.notes: Quote: "a mean excess return of 8.01% a year (Newey-West t-statistic of 3.83), a Sharpe ratio of 0.7848".

relevance.reason: Good record, but not testable with four energy contracts.
